1. Assess the Ailing System: Diagnosing Your Kaba or Gilgen Door Operator

The silent, effortless glide of an automatic door is a hallmark of modern convenience, a piece of engineering so seamlessly integrated into our daily lives that its complexity is often overlooked. When that fluid motion falters—when the door stutters, groans, or ceases to move altogether—it represents more than a simple mechanical failure. It is a disruption of flow, a barrier to access, and a pressing operational challenge for any facility manager. The source of such a problem frequently lies within the heart of the door operator: its motor. For many robust systems, including the widely installed Kaba and Gilgen automatic sliding doors, this core component is a specialized unit often referred to as an SLM motor. The term itself, while sometimes associated with Selective Laser Melting in manufacturing, in this context refers to a specific class of high-performance motor used in door automation. Confronted with a malfunctioning door, the first task is not one of hasty replacement but of careful, reasoned diagnosis. One must become a detective of sorts, observing the symptoms to understand the root cause before prescribing a remedy.

Understanding the Audible and Visible Signs of SLM Motor Failure

Human experience is rich with the capacity for pattern recognition, and diagnosing a failing motor is an exercise in sensing disruptions to an established pattern of smooth operation. The initial signs are often subtle, whispers of a deeper issue. A door that once opened with a quiet hum may now emit a high-pitched whine, a sound that could suggest the bearings within the SLM motor are worn and struggling against increased friction. Think of it as a joint that has lost its cartilage; the movement is still possible, but it is strained and painful.

Alternatively, you might hear a grinding or clicking noise. Such sounds often point toward a problem with the gearbox, the set of gears that translates the high-speed rotation of the SLM motor into the low-speed, high-torque force needed to move a heavy door panel. A stripped gear tooth, for instance, will create a rhythmic clicking as the mechanism attempts to engage but repeatedly slips. Visual cues are equally revealing. Jerky or hesitant movement is a classic symptom. The door might start to open, pause, then lurch forward. This can indicate an inconsistent power delivery from the motor, perhaps due to worn internal components or a failing electronic controller that is integral to the motor's function. In a brushless DC SLM motor, which represents the modern standard, the commutation is handled electronically. A failure in this internal circuitry can lead to the erratic "stepping" motion you observe.

In more severe cases, the door may refuse to move at all, accompanied by a humming sound from the operator housing. This suggests the SLM motor is receiving power and is trying to turn but is mechanically seized or is facing a resistance it cannot overcome. Sometimes, an acrid smell, like burning plastic or electronics, can be detected. This is a definitive sign of a critical electrical failure within the SLM motor windings or its controller, where overheating has begun to break down insulating materials. At this point, continued operation is not only impossible but also hazardous.

The Heart of the Machine: The Role of the SLM Motor in the Broader System

To truly grasp why an SLM motor fails, one must first appreciate its function within the larger organism of the automatic door operator. The SLM motor is not an isolated component; it is the prime mover in a sophisticated electromechanical system. In a typical sliding door operator, such as a Kaba SLM or Gilgen SLH250, the motor is part of a drive unit that includes a gearbox, a drive pulley, and often an integrated electronic controller and encoder. The motor receives a signal from the main control unit, which itself is processing inputs from motion sensors, safety beams, and program switches.

Upon receiving the "open" signal, the controller directs a precise amount of electrical current to the SLM motor. The motor spins at a high RPM (revolutions per minute), but this speed is too fast and its torque (rotational force) is too low to move a door weighing upwards of 100 or 200 kilograms. This is where the gearbox comes in. It acts as a force multiplier, reducing the speed while dramatically increasing the torque. This powerful, controlled rotation is then transferred via a toothed belt to the door carriages, pulling the door panels open or pushing them closed.

An encoder, often a magnetic or optical sensor integrated into the SLM motor assembly, plays a vital role. It constantly reports the motor's exact position, speed, and direction of rotation back to the main controller. This feedback loop allows the controller to know where the door is at all times, enabling it to execute smooth acceleration and deceleration, and to stop precisely at the fully open or closed positions. When you see a door glide to a soft, gentle stop, you are witnessing this feedback system in action. A failure in the encoder can manifest as a door that slams shut, overshoots its mark, or seems "lost" in its travel path. Therefore, a problem that appears to be with the SLM motor might actually stem from its associated encoder.

Preliminary Checks: What to Investigate Before Condemning the Motor

The principle of Occam's razor—that the simplest explanation is often the correct one—is a valuable guide in technical troubleshooting. Before concluding that a costly SLM motor replacement is necessary, a series of simpler checks should be performed. The goal is to eliminate external factors and confirm that the fault is indeed internal to the motor unit itself.

First, ensure the entire operator has power. This may seem elementary, yet it is a common oversight. Check circuit breakers and fuses. Use a multimeter to verify that the correct voltage is reaching the main controller's power input terminals. An unstable or low voltage supply can cause a range of erratic behaviors that mimic motor failure.

Second, inspect the pathway of the door. Is there any physical obstruction? A stone caught in the floor guide, damage to the track, or misaligned door carriages can create immense physical resistance. Disengage the door from the drive belt (most systems have a simple mechanism for this) and try to move it manually. It should slide smoothly with minimal effort. If the door is difficult to move by hand, you have a mechanical problem with the door or track, not the SLM motor. Forcing a motor to work against such resistance is a sure way to cause it to burn out prematurely.

Third, examine the drive belt. Is it properly tensioned? A belt that is too loose can slip on the motor's drive pulley, causing jerky movement. A belt that is too tight places excessive strain on the motor's shaft and bearings, leading to premature wear and audible noise. Check the belt for signs of fraying, cracking, or missing teeth, which would necessitate its replacement.

Finally, consult the main controller. Most modern door operators, like the Dorma/Kaba ES200, have a diagnostic display or a series of LEDs that provide error codes. These codes are an invaluable language for understanding the system's internal state. An error code might explicitly point to a motor fault, but it could just as easily indicate a power supply issue, a sensor failure, or a communication breakdown with a peripheral device. Consulting the operator's technical manual to interpret these codes is a non-negotiable step in a professional diagnosis. Only after these external factors have been systematically ruled out can one confidently point the finger at the SLM motor assembly itself.

2. Define Your Needs: Matching the Motor to the Application

Once the diagnostic process has isolated the fault to the SLM motor, the next phase begins: defining the precise requirements for its replacement. This is not a matter of finding just any motor that fits; it is about selecting a component whose capabilities are in harmony with the demands of its environment and task. An automatic door in a quiet rural library and one at the entrance of a major European airport may look similar, but the demands placed on their respective motors are worlds apart. Choosing the wrong motor is akin to asking a sprinter to run a marathon; failure is not a question of if, but when. A meticulous examination of the technical specifications is the foundation for a lasting and reliable repair.

Decoding the Language of Power: Voltage, Torque, and Duty Cycle

The specifications sheet for an SLM motor can appear as a cryptic list of numbers and units. However, understanding a few key parameters will empower you to make an informed choice.

Voltage (V): This is the electrical potential the motor is designed to operate on. Most automatic door motors, including the Dunkermotoren models often used as the basis for an SLM motor, run on low-voltage DC (Direct Current), typically 24V or 30V. It is absolutely paramount to match the voltage of the replacement motor to the output of the system's power supply and controller. Applying the wrong voltage can have immediate and destructive consequences. Over-voltage will cause the motor to overheat and burn out rapidly, while under-voltage will result in insufficient power, preventing the motor from moving the door effectively.

Torque (Nm): Torque is the rotational force the motor can produce. It is the muscle of the system. Measured in Newton-meters (Nm), it determines the motor's ability to overcome the inertia and friction of the door panel. A heavier door, or one with more friction in its track system, requires a motor with higher torque. A motor with insufficient torque will struggle, strain, and ultimately fail. When evaluating a replacement SLM motor for heavy-duty doors, pay close attention to the rated torque to ensure it meets or exceeds the original's specification.

Duty Cycle: This is perhaps the most misunderstood yet one of the most significant specifications. It is not about how long the motor can run continuously in one go, but rather a measure of its ability to operate intermittently over a period without overheating. It is often expressed as a percentage. For example, a duty cycle of 40% means the motor can run for 4 minutes out of every 10-minute period. For an automatic door, which operates in short bursts, a more useful metric is the number of cycles (one open and one close) per hour or per day it is rated for. An SLM motor intended for a high-traffic commercial entrance, like a supermarket or hospital, must have a high duty cycle rating, indicating it is built with materials and cooling capabilities to withstand thousands of operations daily. A motor with a low duty cycle installed in such an environment will be perpetually operating beyond its thermal limits, leading to a drastically shortened lifespan.

Specification Standard Application (e.g., Small Office) Heavy-Duty Application (e.g., Hospital) Why It Matters
Door Weight Up to 100 kg 150 kg to 250 kg+ Heavier doors require significantly more torque to move.
Required Torque 1.5 - 2.5 Nm 3.0 - 5.0+ Nm Insufficient torque leads to stalling and motor burnout.
Traffic Volume < 500 cycles/day 2,000 - 5,000+ cycles/day High traffic necessitates a higher duty cycle to prevent overheating.
Duty Cycle Rating S3 - 30% S3 - 60% or Continuous Duty Mismatching duty cycle is a primary cause of premature failure.
Operating Speed 0.4 - 0.6 m/s 0.7 - 1.0 m/s Higher speeds require a motor capable of higher RPM under load.

A Tale of Two Doors: Heavy-Duty vs. Standard Applications

The comparison table above illuminates a crucial distinction. The physical properties of the door and its expected usage pattern dictate the class of SLM motor required. A standard application might involve a single-leaf glass door at the entrance to a small professional office. The door is relatively light, and the traffic is moderate. A standard SLM motor, correctly specified for this load and traffic, will perform reliably for many years.

Now, consider a heavy-duty application: a double-leaf, lead-lined door for an X-ray room in a busy hospital. These doors are exceptionally heavy to provide radiation shielding. They are also in constant use by staff and patients. Here, a standard motor would be woefully inadequate. The immense weight demands a motor with very high starting torque. The constant use demands an extremely high duty cycle and robust construction to dissipate heat. The motor for this application will be physically larger, have a more substantial gearbox, and be built from higher-grade materials. Using a standard motor in this scenario would be a false economy, as it would likely fail within months, not years, leading to repeated downtime and replacement costs that far exceed the initial savings. When sourcing a replacement, one must be honest and accurate about the application's demands.

The Operating Environment: How Temperature and Contaminants Affect Performance

The environment in which the door operates also plays a significant role in motor selection. An SLM motor is an electrical device, and like all electronics, it has an optimal operating temperature range. An operator installed on an external doorway in a cold climate will experience very different conditions from one on an internal door in a climate-controlled building. Most motors have an IP (Ingress Protection) rating, which consists of two digits. The first digit indicates protection against solid particles (like dust), and the second indicates protection against liquids.

For example, a motor with an IP44 rating is protected against solid objects larger than 1mm (e.g., most wires, screws) and against water splashing from any direction. For a door on a building exterior exposed to rain, or in an industrial facility with dust or moisture, a higher IP rating is advisable. Dust and debris can work their way into the motor housing, abrading moving parts and clogging ventilation paths, which leads to overheating. Moisture can cause short circuits in the electronics or corrosion on mechanical components. Selecting an SLM motor with an appropriate IP rating for its specific location is a proactive measure that safeguards the investment and ensures its longevity. The physical environment is not a passive backdrop; it is an active participant in the life and performance of the motor.

3. Navigate the Market: OEM vs. High-Quality Alternatives

With a clear understanding of the required specifications, the next challenge is to navigate the marketplace. The decision often boils down to a fundamental choice: should one source the exact Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) part, branded by Kaba or Gilgen, or is it prudent to consider a high-quality compatible alternative? This is not merely a question of price, but a complex consideration of availability, guaranteed performance, and the underlying realities of modern manufacturing. The landscape of spare parts in 2026 is nuanced, and an informed decision requires looking beyond the brand label on the box.

The Perceived Security of Original Equipment Manufacturer (OEM) Parts

There is an undeniable sense of security that comes with purchasing an OEM part. It is the "official" replacement, manufactured or sanctioned by the company that made the original door system. The primary argument for choosing an OEM SLM motor is the guarantee of a perfect match. There is no ambiguity about compatibility; it is designed to be a direct, drop-in replacement. The specifications, physical dimensions, mounting points, and electrical connectors will be identical to the failed unit. This simplifies the replacement process, reducing the risk of installation errors and minimizing downtime.

For facilities operating under strict maintenance protocols or where the equipment is still under a broader system warranty, specifying an OEM part may be a non-negotiable requirement. The manufacturer's warranty on the part itself provides a clear path for recourse if the component is defective. This path can sometimes become complicated when third-party parts are introduced into a system. The OEM part represents a known quantity, a continuation of the original engineering and quality control standards set by the brand. It is a choice that prioritizes certainty and minimizes variables, which can be a perfectly rational and justifiable strategy, especially in critical applications.

A Case for Compatible Components: Evaluating Third-Party Replacements

The alternative to the OEM route is to source a compatible replacement from a specialized third-party supplier. In the past, "third-party" could be a byword for inferior quality, but the market has matured significantly. Reputable suppliers now offer components that are not just "clones," but are engineered to meet or even exceed the performance of the original OEM parts. The primary motivation for exploring this option is often cost. Compatible parts can offer substantial savings compared to their OEM-branded counterparts, without a compromise in quality.

This price difference arises not from inferior materials but from the economics of the supply chain. The OEM does not charge solely for the component; the price also includes their brand markup, marketing costs, and the overhead of their larger corporate structure. A specialized parts supplier, with a leaner operation and a focus on high-volume components, can often provide the same or a better-quality SLM motor for a fraction of the price.

Availability is another compelling reason. OEMs may sometimes have long lead times for specific parts, especially for older systems. A dedicated parts specialist, on the other hand, may have the required motor in stock for immediate dispatch, which is a critical advantage when a main entrance is out of service. Furthermore, some third-party suppliers invest in improving upon original designs. They might use higher-grade bearings or more robust electronic components in their version of an SLM motor, potentially offering a longer service life than the original. The key is to source these parts from a trusted, expert supplier who performs their own rigorous testing and stands behind their products with a solid warranty.

The Power Behind the Name: Understanding the Dunkermotoren Connection

The debate between OEM and alternative parts becomes particularly interesting when one investigates the actual manufacturing origin of the components. Major door system brands like Kaba or Gilgen are primarily system integrators. They design the overall operator, the logic of the controller, and the mechanical framework. However, they do not necessarily manufacture every single component themselves. For highly specialized parts like a high-performance brushless DC motor, they often turn to a specialist manufacturer.

In the world of automatic door motors, one name stands out: Dunkermotoren. This German company, part of AMETEK, is a world leader in advanced motion solutions. For decades, they have been the "motor behind the motor," producing the core drive units for many of the biggest names in the automatic door industry, including Dorma (now dormakaba). The venerable Dorma ES200 operator, for example, is famously powered by a Dunkermotoren GR 63x55 motor.

This is a crucial piece of knowledge. When you buy an OEM-branded SLM motor from Kaba or Gilgen, you are often buying a Dunkermotoren product that has been supplied to them and then re-branded. A specialized parts supplier may source the very same Dunkermotoren motor through a different distribution channel, or they may offer a meticulously engineered alternative that uses a Dunkermotoren motor as its core. In this light, the distinction between "original" and "alternative" becomes blurred. The question is not so much about the brand on the outside of the casing, but about the quality of the engineering on the inside. By understanding this supply chain, one can make a more strategic choice, potentially acquiring the exact same level of German engineering found in an OEM part but without the associated brand premium. This knowledge transforms the purchasing decision from a simple brand choice into a sophisticated value judgment.

4. Verify Compatibility and Performance: The Vetting Process

Having decided on a strategic path—be it OEM or a high-quality alternative—the process enters a critical validation phase. A purchase order should not be placed on assumption alone. Verification is the bridge between identifying a need and fulfilling it successfully. This stage is about meticulous cross-referencing, demanding evidence of performance, and evaluating the human expertise that stands behind the product. It is an intellectual due diligence that protects against incorrect orders, installation headaches, and the frustration of a part that does not perform as expected. This vetting process ensures that the component arriving at your facility is not just a part in a box, but the correct solution to your problem.

The Art of the Match: Cross-Referencing Part Numbers and System Models

The single most effective tool for ensuring compatibility is the part number. The original, failed SLM motor will almost certainly have a label or an etching on its casing with a series of alphanumeric codes. This is its identity. The primary code will be the one assigned by the door system manufacturer (e.g., Kaba or Gilgen). There might also be a secondary number from the actual component manufacturer (like Dunkermotoren). It is essential to record all of these numbers accurately.

When approaching a supplier, this part number is your primary query. For an OEM part, the process is straightforward: the numbers should match exactly. When considering an alternative, the supplier must be able to confirm that their product is a direct cross-reference to the original OEM part number. A reputable supplier will have an extensive database for this purpose. They should be able to say, "Yes, our model XYZ is the direct replacement for Kaba part number 12345."

Do not rely on visual comparison alone. Two motors might look nearly identical but have different internal windings for different voltages, or different gear ratios in the gearbox. Beyond the part number, you should also provide the model of the door operator system (e.g., Gilgen SLH250, Kaba SLM) and, if possible, its serial number or year of manufacture. Systems can undergo revisions over their production life, and a motor for a 2018 model might be slightly different from one for a 2024 model. Providing the supplier with this complete set of information allows them to pinpoint the exact replacement with a high degree of confidence, eliminating guesswork. It is a collaborative effort: you provide the detailed information from the field, and the supplier provides the expert knowledge from their database.

Beyond the Label: Seeking Technical Data Sheets and Performance Guarantees

A trustworthy supplier will do more than just promise compatibility; they will provide evidence. The gold standard of evidence is the technical data sheet. This document, typically a PDF, is the motor's full resume. It lists all the critical specifications discussed earlier: rated voltage and current, no-load and rated speed, rated torque, gear ratio, duty cycle, IP rating, and dimensional drawings.

You should request the data sheet for the proposed replacement SLM motor and compare it meticulously against the data sheet for the original motor, if you can find it. If the original's data sheet is unavailable, compare the replacement's specs against the known requirements of your application. Does the torque meet the needs of your heavy door? Is the duty cycle appropriate for your high-traffic entrance? Do the dimensional drawings confirm that the mounting holes and shaft diameter are identical?

This step is particularly important when evaluating an alternative part. The data sheet is the supplier's commitment in writing. It is a statement of fact about the product's capabilities. A supplier who is hesitant or unable to provide a detailed data sheet should be viewed with caution. It may suggest they lack a deep technical understanding of their own products or that the product itself is not subject to rigorous quality control and documentation. Performance guarantees, such as certified testing results for cycle life or noise levels, are further indicators of a high-quality product from a confident supplier.

The Human Element: The Importance of Supplier Expertise and Support

In an increasingly automated world, the value of genuine human expertise cannot be overstated. The final and perhaps most telling step in the vetting process is to engage with the supplier's technical support team. The quality of this interaction is a powerful indicator of the quality of the company as a whole.

When you contact them, are you met with a salesperson reading from a script, or a knowledgeable technician who understands the nuances of automatic door systems? Can they answer detailed questions? For example, you could ask: "My current Kaba SLM motor has a 7-pin connector. Your replacement shows a 7-pin connector in the photo, but can you confirm the pinout is identical to the Kaba standard to ensure it communicates correctly with my existing controller?" or "I've noticed my original motor tends to run hot. Does your alternative model incorporate any specific features for better thermal dissipation?"

A truly expert supplier, like the team at DoorDynamic, will not only be able to answer these questions but may also offer proactive advice. They might ask you about your application to confirm you are selecting the right model, or they might suggest checking the power supply as a potential related issue. This level of engagement shows that they are not just moving boxes; they are problem-solvers. They are invested in your success because their reputation depends on the reliable performance of their components in the field. This technical dialogue builds trust and provides assurance that if you encounter an issue during installation, you will have a competent resource to call upon. A good part from a supplier with poor support can be just as problematic as a poor part. The ideal is to find a high-quality component backed by high-quality human expertise.

5. Secure Your Purchase: Sourcing from a Reliable Supplier in 2026

The final phase of the process is the transaction itself—transforming research and verification into a tangible solution arriving at your doorstep. This is more than a simple act of purchasing. It is about establishing a relationship with a supplier who can be a long-term partner in maintaining the operational integrity of your facility's access points. In the European market of 2026, selecting the right supplier involves looking at their business practices, their commitment to customer support, and the logistical efficiency of their operation. A successful purchase is one that is smooth, transparent, and provides peace of mind long after the installation is complete.

Hallmarks of a Dependable European Parts Supplier

What separates an exceptional supplier from a merely adequate one? Several key characteristics serve as hallmarks of reliability and professionalism, particularly within the European context.

First, transparency and depth of information. A dependable supplier’s website is not just a storefront; it is a resource. Look for clear, high-resolution photos of the products from multiple angles. Vague or generic stock photos are a red flag. The product descriptions should be detailed, listing not just the part name but also the key specifications and the OEM part numbers it is designed to replace. Companies like DoorDynamic offer a clear catalog of SLM motor components that exemplifies this transparency.

Second, a clear physical presence and accessible contact information. A trustworthy business is not anonymous. Look for a clear company address, a local European phone number, and a professional email address. This indicates an established entity that is accountable and reachable.

Third, specialization and focus. A supplier who specializes in automatic door parts is likely to have deeper knowledge and a more relevant inventory than a generalist industrial parts warehouse. Their focus means they understand the specific challenges and requirements of your application. They speak your language.

Finally, consider their logistical capabilities. Do they hold stock in Europe for fast delivery? In an urgent repair situation, waiting weeks for a part to ship from another continent is not a viable option. A European supplier should be able to offer clear shipping timelines and costs, with options for express delivery when downtime is critical. They should also demonstrate an understanding of cross-border trade within the EU, ensuring a smooth and predictable delivery process.

Peace of Mind: Warranty, Returns, and After-Sales Service

A supplier's confidence in their product is most tangibly expressed through their warranty. A one-year warranty is a common standard, but a supplier offering a two-year or even longer warranty on a component like an SLM motor is making a powerful statement about its quality and durability. Before purchasing, read the warranty terms carefully. Is it a simple replacement warranty? Does it cover shipping costs? What is the process for making a claim? A clear, straightforward warranty process is a sign of a customer-focused company.

Equally important is the return policy. What happens if you mistakenly order the wrong part, or if the diagnosis was incorrect and the motor was not the issue? A flexible and fair return policy provides a crucial safety net. It shows that the supplier understands the realities of maintenance work and is willing to work with their customers to find a solution, rather than simply closing the sale.

After-sales service is the ongoing support you receive after the purchase. This is where the value of the technical expertise discussed earlier truly comes to fruition. If your installer has a question during the fitting process, can they call a support line and speak to someone who can help? This level of support can be the difference between a quick, successful repair and a prolonged, frustrating ordeal. It transforms the supplier from a mere vendor into a valuable technical partner.

The Final Step: Ordering and Preparing for a Successful Installation

Once you have selected a supplier and a product that meets all these criteria, the ordering process should be straightforward. A professional e-commerce platform will allow for secure payment and provide immediate confirmation and an invoice.

With the order placed, the final step is to prepare for the part's arrival. This is a moment to ensure efficiency and safety. Schedule the installation with a qualified technician. While a competent in-house maintenance person can often perform the replacement, automatic doors are heavy and can be dangerous if not handled correctly. Ensure the technician has the correct tools and has reviewed the installation guide for the door operator.

When the new SLM motor arrives, inspect it immediately. Does it match what you ordered? Is there any sign of shipping damage? It is far better to identify an issue at this stage than after the old motor has been removed.

The installation process itself should be methodical. The first step is always to disconnect the power to the operator at the circuit breaker. The technician will then relieve the belt tension, remove the old motor assembly, mount the new one, reconnect the electrical plugs, and re-tension the belt correctly. After restoring power, the system will likely need to perform a "learn cycle," where the controller moves the door slowly from fully closed to fully open to learn the door's travel distance and mass. The technician should then test all functions: the activation sensors, the safety beams, and the operation from any program switches. A successful installation concludes with the door returning to its state of quiet, reliable, and effortless motion—the problem solved, and normal operations restored.

Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ)

1. Is an SLM motor the same as a motor for a Dorma ES200? In many cases, they are fundamentally very similar or even identical. "SLM motor" often refers to the drive units used in Kaba and Gilgen systems, while the ES200 uses a specific Dunkermotoren model (like the GR 63x55). Both are typically high-quality DC motors, often brushless, made by specialist manufacturers. The key is to match the exact part number or have a supplier confirm cross-compatibility, as housings and connectors can differ even if the core motor is the same.

2. Can I replace just the motor, or do I need the entire motor/gearbox assembly? It is strongly recommended to replace the entire motor and gearbox assembly as a single unit. The motor and gearbox are precisely mated at the factory. Attempting to separate them and replace only the motor can be difficult, and a worn gearbox will cause a new motor to fail prematurely. Most suppliers sell them as a complete, sealed "drive unit" for this reason, ensuring reliability.

3. How long should a new SLM motor last? The lifespan of an SLM motor depends heavily on the application and proper installation. In a standard-traffic environment with a correctly specified motor, a lifespan of 7-10 years or over a million cycles is a reasonable expectation. In a very high-traffic, heavy-duty application, the lifespan might be closer to 3-5 years. Premature failure is almost always due to under-specification (wrong motor for the job), poor installation, or issues with power supply or track resistance.

4. My old motor was a brushed DC motor. Can I replace it with a modern brushless one? This is generally not a direct swap. Brushed and brushless motors require different types of controllers. A brushless motor has its commutation handled electronically and needs a controller designed for it. If you are upgrading from a very old system with a brushed motor, you will likely need to replace the motor, the main controller, and potentially the power supply as a "retrofit kit" to ensure all components can communicate and work together.

5. What are the most common mistakes to avoid when replacing an SLM motor? The most common mistakes are: 1) Misdiagnosing the problem and replacing a healthy motor when the issue was the power supply or a mechanical obstruction. 2) Ordering the wrong part by relying on visual appearance instead of matching part numbers. 3) Failing to properly re-tension the drive belt after installation—too loose causes slipping, too tight causes strain. 4) Neglecting to perform the system's "learn cycle" after installation, which can lead to erratic operation.

Conclusion

The journey from a faltering automatic door to a fully restored system is a process of disciplined inquiry and methodical action. It begins not with a purchase, but with an investigation—a careful observation of symptoms to arrive at an accurate diagnosis. It proceeds through a thoughtful analysis of the application's unique demands, translating the physical reality of door weight and foot traffic into the technical language of torque and duty cycle. This clarity allows for an informed navigation of the market, weighing the security of OEM parts against the compelling value and quality offered by reputable alternative suppliers. The critical vetting stage, grounded in the cross-referencing of part numbers and the scrutiny of technical data, provides the necessary assurance of compatibility and performance. Finally, by selecting a knowledgeable and supportive European supplier, the purchase itself becomes more than a transaction; it is the culmination of a diligent process and the beginning of a reliable, long-term solution. By following this five-point framework, a facility manager or technician in 2026 can approach the task of replacing an SLM motor not as a reactive emergency, but as a controlled and professional exercise in asset management, ensuring safety, access, and operational continuity.

    Instructions for safe operation

    • Failure to observe the information in this manual may result in personal injury or damage to equipment.
    • To reduce the risk of injury of persons - use this operator only with pedestrian doors.
    • Do not use the equipment if repair or adjustment is necessary.
    • Disconnect supply when cleaning or other maintenance is to be carried out.
    • The operator can be used by children age 8 and above, and persons with reduced physical, sensory or mental capabilities, or lack of experience and knowledge, if they have been given supervision or instruction by a person responsible for their safety concerning safe operator use and the possible hazards involved.
    • This does not however prevent those persons to use the door where the operator is installed.
    • Cleaning and user maintenance shall not be made by children without supervision.
    • Do not let children climb on or play with the door or the fixed/remote controls.
    • Installer must properly ground door package! Improper grounding can lead to risk of personal injury.
    • The doorset can be operated automatically by sensors or manually by activators.

    Congratulations on your new automatic door!

    ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems has developed automatic doors for more than 50 years. State-of-the-art technology and carefully tested materials and components provide you with a superior product.

    As with all other technical products, your automatic door requires periodic maintenance and service. It is essential that you know your automatic door (system) and that you recognize the importance of maintaining it in compliance with applicable standards for safety.

    Your local ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems-authorized representative is familiar with these standards, as well as all applicable local codes and ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems recommendations for power-operated pedestrian doors. Service and adjustments performed by your ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems-authorized representative, will ensure safe and proper operation of your automatic door unit.

    Electronic equipment reception interference

    The equipment complies with the European EMC directive (US market FCC Part 15), provided installed according to Installation and Service manual.

    The equipment may generate and use radio frequency energy and if not installed and used properly, it may cause interference to radio, television reception or other radio frequency type systems.

    If other equipment does not fully comply with immunity requirements interference may occur. There is no guarantee that interference will not occur in a particular installation. If this equipment does cause interference to radio or television reception, which can be determined by turning the equipment off and on, the user is encouraged to try to correct the interference by one or more of the following measures:

    • Re-orient the receiving antenna.
    • Relocate the receiver with respect to the equipment.
    • Move the receiver away from the equipment.
    • Plug the receiver into a different outlet so that equipment and receiver are on different branch circuits.
    • Check that protective earth (PE) is connected.

    If necessary, the user should consult the dealer or an experienced electronics technician for additional suggestions.

    Environmental requirements

    ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems products are equipped with electronics and may also be equipped with batteries containing materials which are hazardous to the environment. Disconnect power before removing electronics and battery and make sure it is disposed of properly according to local regulations (how and where) as was done with the packaging material.

    Product liability

    According to regulations, the following are the responsibility of the owner or caretaker of the equipment:

    • that the equipment operates correctly, so that it gives sufficient protection in regard to safety and health
    • that the equipment is operated and regularly maintained, inspected and serviced by someone with documented competence in the equipment and in applicable regulations
    • that the provided “Service Log Book” and “Site Acceptance Test and Risk Assessment” documents (PRA-0005) are kept available for maintenance and service records
    • that inspection covers the emergency opening function (when applicable)
    • that the closing force is appropriate for the door size on fire-approved door systems (when applicable)

    Warranty

    ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems warrants its products to be free from defects in material and workmanship under intended use and service for a warranty time of 12 months, beginning at time of delivery. This warranty extends only to the original buyer of the equipment.

    ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems warrants that the software will operate substantially in accordance with its functional descriptions and that it has been recorded on non-defective media.

    The ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems warranty does not apply to:

    • That the software will be error-free or operate without interruption
    • General wear and tear on the system
    • Fuse, disposable batteries and glass damage
    • System deviations caused by installer other than ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems
    • System that has been altered or damaged by vandalism or misuse
    • System that has been additionally equipped with non-ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems original branded parts and/or spare parts
    • Unrequired visits due to poor client communication (door working when our technician arrives, reset, power discontinuation)
    • Adjustments (closing and opening speed and also detection field radars) due to customer requests (excludes operational adjustments thought to create a hazard)
    • Water damage
    • Adverse weather conditions
    • Any damage caused, directly or indirectly, by a circumstance beyond the control of the applicable company within ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems, such as industrial dispute, fire, natural disaster, war, extensive military mobilization, insurrection, requisition, seizure, embargo, restrictions in the use of power and defects or delays in deliveries by sub-contractors caused by any such circumstances

    Service

    Regular inspections by a trained and qualified person, and the frequency of service occasions, should at minimum be made according to national regulations or industry standard, in the absence of a national regulation. This is especially important when the installation concerns a fire-approved door or a door with an emergency-opening function. To extend the life of your investment and ensure safe and reliable operation of the door, we recommend a minimum of 2 visits per year or more, depending on usage and operating conditions. Environmental aspects shall also be considered.

    Intended use

    The Besam SL500, Besam SL500 T and Besam SL500 SL are automatic sliding door operators developed to facilitate entrances to buildings and within buildings through sliding doors.

    The door is designed to offer continuous use, a high degree of safety and maximum lifetime. The system is self-adjusting to the effects caused by normal variations in the weather conditions and to minor friction changes caused by e.g. dust and dirt.

    In emergency situations the doorset is opened and remains open automatically. It may also be equipped with break-out function, in which case the door leaf is pushed manually open in the escape direction.

    Dual batteries and motors are used in escape routes as indicated in associated certificates.

    It is to be used indoors where it is suitable for almost all types of external and internal sliding doors. Ensure that the lock is only activated when there are no persons in the room.

    For installation and maintenance see Installation and Service manual 1009203. Save these instructions for future reference.

    Technical specification

    • Manufacturer: ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems AB
    • Address: Lodjursgatan 10, SE-261 44 Landskrona, Sweden
    • Type: Sliding Door Operator Besam SL500, Besam SL500 T and Besam SL500 SL
    • Mains power supply: 100 V AC -10% to 240 V AC +10%, 50/60 Hz, fuse 10 AT
    • Power consumption: Max. 250 W
    • Degree of protection: IP20
    • Approvals: Third party approvals from established certification organizations valid for safety in use, see Declaration of Conformity.

    How the Besam SL500, Besam SL500 T and Besam SL500 SL work

    The Besam SL500, Besam SL500 T and Besam SL500 SL work electromechanically. The motor, control unit, transmission – and optional emergency unit and electromechanical locking device – are all assembled in a support beam with an integrated cover. The motor and gear box transmit movement to the door leaves by means of a tooth belt. The door leaf is fitted to a door adapter/carriage wheel fitting and hangs on a sliding track. The guiding at the bottom is carried out by means of floor guides, (Full Break-Out) or Side Panel Guides (Fixed Sidelites).

    When an OPENING IMPULSE is received by the control unit the motor starts and transmits movement to the door leaves, which move to the open position.

    The closing starts when no OPENING IMPULSE is received and the HOLD OPEN TIME has expired.

    Locking

    Doors used for emergency escape in buildings such as hospitals and homes for elderly people may not be locked or put in programme selection OFF mode. In other buildings emergency escape doors may be locked or put in programme selection OFF mode after it has been secured and all people have left the building.

    Unlocking

    Unlock all the mechanical locks before activating the operator.

    Operation mode selectors

    The door functions are set with different operate mode selectors. The operation mode selector is available with 5 buttons (plus RESET). The key on the PSK-6U mode selector must always be removed on emergency escape doors after changing settings.

    Functions

    OPEN, AUTO PARTIAL, AUTO, ONE WAY and OFF functions can be obtained.

    Symbol Text Function
    - OPEN The door is permanently open. The door can be moved by hand e.g. for window cleaning. All activation units except for the emergency push button (if fitted) are disconnected.
    - AUTO PARTIAL Two-way traffic, AUTO PARTIAL is obtained. The door can be opened partially with the inner and outer activation units and with a key switch (if fitted). With an emergency push-button the door opens fully.
    - AUTO Two-way traffic, normal operation of the door. The door can be opened with the inner and outer activation units and with a key switch/emergency push-button (if fitted).
    - ONE WAY Passage from inside only. The door is normally locked if an electromechanical locking device has been fitted. The door can only be opened with the inner activation unit or with a key switch/emergency push-button (if fitted).
    R OFF This function is only used on emergency escape doors after it is certain that all people have left the building. The door cannot be opened with inner and outer activation units. The door is locked if an electromechanical locking device has been fitted. The door can be opened partially with a key switch (if fitted). With an emergency pushbutton (if fitted) the door opens fully. (See full manual for details on arrow down operation).
    - RESET

    By briefly pushing the globe of the logotype with a narrow object, the door operator will make a RESET function with a system test. The door will return to the closed position (if not in operation mode selection OPEN or if an error is present) and is then ready for normal operation.

    PSK-6U: Turn the key clockwise to the position “R” (six o’clock) and insert a narrow object in the small hole on the operation mode selector and push briefly. Then turn the key counter-clockwise back to the requested setting and the door operator will make a RESET function with a system test.

    Access codes and flashing light

    Codes

    1. The default access is obtained by pushing the arrow symbol pointing up or down for 2 seconds.
    2. An optional access code can be selected where the access is obtained by briefly pushing in turn the arrow up symbol, followed by the arrow down symbol, followed by the arrow down symbol again and at last the arrow up. The entire code must be entered within 3 seconds.
    3. No access code.

    Flashing light

    • Red: A red light every other second is indicating an error in the door operator. If the error remains after a RESET then service is needed. If the red light is quickly flashing 3 times per second it is indicating an internal error in the operation mode selector.
    • Orange: An orange light every other second is indicating a status or condition that can be cleared by the owner e.g. a break-out door is standing open.
    • Yellow: A yellow light every other second is indicating that maintenance is needed.

    Integrated safety

    To permit a safe passage between closing doors, the doors reverse immediately if an obstruction is detected. They then resume their interrupted movement at low speed to check whether the obstruction has disappeared or not. If an obstruction is detected between opening doors and surrounding walls or interior fittings, the doors stop immediately, and then close after a time delay.

    Technologically advanced sensors

    The ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems sensors have been tested and approved by the ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems test laboratory. Monitored sensors have built-in monitoring for error detection.

    Note! If you have a problem you cannot correct, turn off the automatic door immediately and call your ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems service representative for assistance.

    How to check your inner and outer combined motion and presence detection sensors

    Combined sensors are used when you want both a motion sensor and a presence sensor integrated into the same unit.

    1. When walking towards the door opening at moderate speed, the door should start opening when you are about 1.5 meter from the door. It shall slide open smoothly and stop in the fully open position.
    2. Repeat the same procedure from the other side of the door opening. Move slowly through the door (about 15 cm/s). The door shall remain open.
    3. If your door is set up for one-way traffic, the sensor on the side not intended for use shall reopen the closing door if an object is detected at a minimum of 20 cm from the door at floor level.
    4. Step out of the detection field. After a short time delay the door shall slide closed smoothly.
    5. Walk parallel to the inner door face (about 80 cm from the door face) to check that your motion is detected during at least the complete door opening width. Repeat the same procedure on the outer door face.
    6. Open the door and move your hand from one side (right/left) into the inner door face presence field. Keep it motionless for several seconds at about 30 cm over the floor level. The door should remain open as long as you are within the detection area. Repeat the same procedure on the outer door face.

    How to check your side presence detector(s)

    Side presence sensors are used for example if higher door speed is required or for installations in homes for elderly/disabled or childcare centres, to protect users from being struck by the doors during their opening cycle. When a side presence sensor detects an obstacle the door operator will not stop, but slow down the door movement to a quite safe speed. With this safe speed the door will try to push the obstruction away of the opening door. Make sure that the door starts to open.

    1. Walk into the detection field of the side presence sensor on one side. The door shall not stop, but slow down to safe speed during the opening.
    2. If you have a bi-parting (double) door then repeat the procedure above on the other side.

    Safety system with photocells

    Alternatively the safety system can incorporate presence photocells in the door opening. If an object is breaking the infrared (invisible) beam between the photocell units, while the doors are closing, the doors reverse immediately. They then resume their interrupted movement as soon as the object is removed.

    Emergency escape

    The operator can be fitted with different emergency escape units to ensure a safe evacuation of the building.

    Break-out unit PSB

    The door leaves and the side screens are swung outwards when a defined pressure is applied. The break-out function can also be used to create a wider opening. From the fully swung out position, the door leaves can be manually slid sideways, offering the possibility to transport wide objects through the opening, or to make a shop entrance more inviting during good weather.

    Electrical emergency unit

    The door is opened by means of a rechargeable battery unit in the event of a power failure. The door remains in this position until the power is restored. The operator will then resume the function set by the programme selector. The emergency unit is monitored by the operator control unit. A monitoring error means that the door opens and remains open until the error is cleared. The electrical emergency function can also be used to close the door in the event of power failure. The fire authorities make this a requirement to stop fire or smoke from spreading throughout the building.

    Regular safety checks

    have a problem you cannot correct, turn off the automatic door immediately and call your ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems service representative for assistance.

    Regular safety checks

    To help you fulfil the national/international requirements and to avoid malfunction and risk for injuries, we have provided the following checklist. Do not use if repair or adjustment is necessary. Disconnect supply when cleaning or other maintenance is to be carried out.

    Daily Action

    • Activate your operator and visually check fastening and any damage of:
      • operator and cover
      • cables
      • operator mode selector(s)
      • door and glass (stability)
    • Also inspect your operator and check visually for:
      • condition of door seals and weather stripping
      • condition of glazing rubbers
      • finger protection
      • proper operation (closes slowly and smoothly)
      • any ventilation being obstructed
    • Set the programme selector to OFF and check that the operator and electromechanical lock (if fitted) work together. Also check that the lock really secures the door.
    • Activate the manual activation units, if any, and walk towards the door. Check that the door has opened appropriately while you pass the entrance/exit.
    • Then proceed with the automatic activation units in the same way.
    • Check the safety sensors.

    Escape doors

    If the operator is equipped with break-out system, set the programme selector to AUTO mode. Push the door manually while in the escape direction to ensure that nothing prevents the door from being open. Also ensure that the escape route is free for use. After the test, restore the door(s) to their normal mode of operation.

    Fire doors

    If the operator is equipped with automatic opening system, shut off the power and the door should open and remain open. Restore power and the door should close. Let the door close after an impulse ensuring nothing prevents the door from closing and locking (if regulations require it).

    If problem occurs: Take appropriate measures or contact your ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems representative.

    Cleaning

    The best way to remove dust and dirt from the Besam SL500, Besam SL500 T and Besam SL500 SL is to use water and a soft cloth or a sponge.

    • Do not expose windows, doors or profiles to alkalis. Both aluminium and glass are sensitive to alkalis.
    • Do not clean with high pressure water. Operator, programme selector and sensor may be damaged and water may enter the profiles.
    • Do not use polishing detergent.
    • Do not scrub with materials like Scotch-brite, as this will cause mechanical damage.

    A gentle detergent may be used. To maintain the quality of the enamel layer, the surfaces should be cleaned once/four months period. The cleaning should be documented. To avoid damages to the profiles the brushes/weather stripping must be vacuum-cleaned weekly.

    Signage

    Check that all required signage is applied and intact. Mandatory indicates that the signage is required by European directives and equivalent national legislation outside the European Union.

    • Product label: Mandatory
    • Emergency break-out: Mandatory, if approved for escape route.
    • ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems door sticker: Mandatory, if applicable to highlight the presence of the glass (applied to all glass sections that are moving).
    • Supervision of child: Mandatory, if applicable (applied to both sides of the door). To be placed on entrances where the risk analysis shows use by children, elderly and disabled.
    • Operator designed for disabled people: Recommended, if applicable (applied to both sides of the door).
    • Activation by disabled people: Recommended, if applicable.
    • No entry, identifying one-way traffic: Mandatory in GB and US, if applicable (applied to the side of the door not intended for entry).
    • Automatic door
    • Keep clear

    Safety accessories

    Even though the Besam SL500, Besam SL500 T and Besam SL500 SL are installed to comply with all applicable safety regulations, it is possible to enhance safety/comfort with the following add-ons (please contact your local ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems company for detailed description).

    • Combined motion and presence sensors
    • Separate presence sensors

    General accessories

    Your Besam SL500, Besam SL500 T and Besam SL500 SL can be further improved with the following add-ons (please contact your local ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems dealer for detailed description).

    Cover

    Made in clear anodized aluminium as standard. Paint finished in RAL colours or anodizing optional.

    Motion sensors

    Motion and presence sensors, see separate manuals or installation drawings.

    Operation mode selectors

    See page 9 and separate installation drawing 1013675.

    Electrical locks

    There are 4 different types of locks to the operator. Locked with power (LDP), fail safe, locked without power (LD), fail secure or bistable lock (LDB) and espagnolette lock (LDE).

    Note! The espagnolette lock is at the moment not aloud to mount in escape routs.

    Manual Opening Lock device, MOLD

    For manual unlocking of the electrical lock (LD), locked without power (fail safe).

    See separate installation drawing 1013736.

    Micro switch kit

    For indication of door and lock position. Old version of LSK.

    Locked door indicator

    For indication of locked lock and closed door for connection to alarm system.

    Electrical emergency unit with batteries

    Used if a door is required to be opened or closed by means of a rechargeable battery unit and remain in this position in the event of power failure. Authorities can demand that the emergency units are monitored on a regular time basis. Half an hour before this time has elapsed the following opening impulse generates an emergency opening test. If there is no opening impulse within the next half hour, the operator control unit generates the opening impulse itself.

    If the battery opens the door within the limited time the test is successful and the door resumes the function set by the operation mode selector.

    Note! The test is never performed in operation mode selector setting OPEN. In setting OFF it can be selected. The test is always performed after a RESET and after changing operation mode selection, from a position where a test is not done to a position where the test is a demand.

    Electrical emergency unit with batteries and two motors

    Used if a door is required to be opened by means of a rechargeable battery unit and remain in this position in the event of power failure. Authorities can demand that the emergency unit is monitored on a regular time basis. Half an hour before this time has elapsed the following opening impulse generates an emergency opening test. If there is no opening impulse within half an hour, the operator control unit generates the opening impulse itself.

    If the battery opens the door within the limited time the test is successful and the door resumes the function set by the operation mode selector.

    Note! The test is never performed in operation mode selector setting OPEN. In setting OFF it can be selected. The test is always performed after a RESET and after changing operation mode selection, from a position where a test is not done to a position where the test is a demand.

    Emergency closing with repeated closing

    If the door is opened by hand after an electrical emergency closing, it will close again.

    Break-out unit PSB

    Enables door/side screens to be broken outwards in case of emergency. See page 16.

    Interlocking

    Used between two operators when the first operator must close before the other one can open (typical to reduce energy losses and not for security reasons). Interconnecting cable required.

    Convenience battery UPS

    Stand-by supply which gives continued operation during short power failure.

    External error indication

    Obtained if a lamp or a buzzer is connected.

    Key switches (flush and/or surface mounted)

    Used to give opening impulse to the door in any operation mode selector setting. With electrical emergency unit also during power failure.

    Push button

    Used to give opening impulse to the door. See separate installation drawing 656005.

    Synchronization

    Used between the operators of two single sliding doors, working together in very large openings. Interconnecting cable required.

    Troubleshooting

    What´s wrong? Remedies
    The door does not open
    The motor does not start
    • Change the setting of the program selector.
    • If break-out unit PSB is installed, check that the door leaves and side screens are completely closed.
    • Check the mains switch and fuse in the building.
    The door does not open
    The motor starts but stops during opening
    • Unlock the mechanical locks.
    • Clean the floor guide.
    • Check for objects jammed under the door.
    The door does not close
    The motor does not start
    • Change the setting of the program selector.
    • If a presence sensor is installed, check for and remove objects placed in the presence zone.
    The door does not close
    The motor starts but stops during opening
    • Clean the floor guide.
    • Check for objects jammed under the door.
    The door moves slowly
    • Prevent traffic using the door and allow it to do a complete opening and closing cycle with low speed.
    • Reset the operator by pushing the AUTO-symbol on the mode selector and then push a narrow object on the globe of the logotype on the operator mode selector.
    • Allow the operator to control the closed position without interruption.

    If the problem continues, please contact your ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems representative.

    Service/Maintenance

    Service and adjustments performed by your ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems-authorized representative will ensure safe and proper operation of your automatic door unit.

    Remember to keep “Service Log Book” and “Site Acceptance Test and Risk Assessment” documents (PRA-0005) available. These are used together.

    The table below shows the recommended interval in months, when to replace parts during preventive maintenance. Talk to your ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems representative to learn more about our service offering.

    Part Low traffic
    <10 cycles/hour    		 Medium traffic
    <100 cycles/hour    		 High traffic
    >100 cycles/hour    		 Abusive Environment
    Electrical emergency unit battery 24 months 24 months 24 months 24 months
    Floor guide shoe (Standard/Break-out) 24 months 12 months 6 months 6 months
    Door carriage wheels (Plastic/Steel) 36 months 24 months 12 months 12 months
    Anti-riser device 48 months 36 months 24 months 12 months
    Sliding track 60 months 48 months 36 months 24 months
    Tooth belt - - - -

    Other products from ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems

    • Door Systems
    • Balance doors
    • Air curtains
    • Revolving doors
    • Swing doors
    • Automatic and manual activation units
    • Service such as preventive maintenance and upgrade programs, emergency repairs, service advice and door management

    Declaration of conformity

    ASSA ABLOY Entrance Systems AB declares under our sole responsibility that the type of equipment: Besam SL500, Besam SL500 T, Besam SL500 SL, Besam SL500 ADS, Besam SL500 T ADS, Besam SL500 SL ADS. With or without emergency unit.

    • Complies with the following directives: 2004/108/EC ElectroMagnetic Compatibility Directive (EMCD), 2006/42/EC Machinery Directive (MD).
    • Harmonized European standards which have been applied: EN 60335-1, EN 61000-6-2, EN 61000-6-3, EN ISO 13849-1, EN 16005.
    • Other standards or technical specifications, which have been applied: BBR, BVL, FCC 47 CFR Part 15 B, IEC 60335-1, UL 325, EN 60335-2-103, IEC 60335-2-103.

    EC type examination or certificate issued by a notified or competent body:
    RU D-SE.A730.B.02565

    The manufacturing process ensures the compliance of the equipment with the technical file. The manufacturing process is regularly assessed by 3rd party.

ES 200 Easy / ES 200 / ES 200-2D

Title: GEZE Powerdrive DCU1-NT & DCU1-2M-NT User Manual
Author: leo lu
Body HTML:
GEZE Powerdrive DCU1 Controller

 

1. Introduction

These instructions contain important information regarding the operation and maintenance of the GEZE Powerdrive automatic sliding door systems, including components like the GEZE DCU1-NT controller.

1.1 Symbols and Illustrations

Warning notices are used in these instructions to warn you of personal injury and property damage. Always read and observe these warning notices. Observe all the measures that are marked with the warning symbol and warning word.

WARNING

Danger to persons. Non-compliance may result in death or serious injuries.

CAUTION

Danger to persons. Non-compliance can result in minor to medium injuries.

Additional Symbols

Symbol Meaning
Important Note Information about avoiding property damage.
Additional Information Useful additional information. There is no danger to persons or property.
Action Symbol This means you have to do something. If there are several actions, keep to the given order.
BOBO (Break-out) The door leaves and side panels are equipped with a break-out function.
No BOBO No break-out function; means the function is not possible for break-out doors.

1.2 Product Liability

In accordance with the manufacturer's liability for their products as defined in the German “Produkthaftungsgesetz” (Product Liability Act), the information contained in this user manual (product information and proper use, misuse, product performance, product maintenance, obligations to provide information and instructions) is to be noted and followed. Failure to comply releases the manufacturer from his statutory liability.

1.3 Special Cases

In certain cases, deviations from the information given in this user manual may occur. Examples include:

  • Special wiring
  • Special function settings (parameters)
  • Special software

Please contact the service technician responsible for further information.

1.4 More Detailed Information

Information for commissioning and maintenance can be found in the wiring diagram and in the installation instructions for the various automatic sliding doors.

1.5 Terms

Activation device inside (KI)
Push button, switch or movement detector for activating the GEZE DCU1 door drive. The activation device is located within the room enclosed by the door. Active in “Automatic” and “Exit only” modes. No function in “Night/Locked” and “Off” modes.
Activation device outside (KA)
Push button, switch or movement detector for activating the door drive. The activation device is located outside the room enclosed by the door. Active in “Automatic” mode. No function in “Exit only”, “Night/Locked” and “Off” modes.
Activation device authorised (KB)
Access control function (e.g., key switch or card reader) used by authorised persons to activate the door drive. Active in all modes: “Automatic”, “Exit only”, “Night/Locked” and “Off”.
Opening safety sensor (SIO)
Presence detector (e.g., active infrared light sensor) for protecting the swinging range of the door in the opening direction. The sensor secures the secondary closing edge.
Closing safety sensor (SIS)
Presence detector (e.g., active infrared light sensor) for protecting the swinging range of the door in the closing direction. The sensor secures the main closing edge on the inside and outside.
Emergency stop
Self-locking switch with which immediate stopping of the door drive can be triggered in case of danger. The door drive remains in its current position until the user releases the emergency stop switch again.
Emergency lock
When the emergency lock is triggered, the door is closed and locked. The activations and safety devices are deactivated during the closing process.
Reset
Push button for restarting the drive after the operating voltage has been switched on or after a fire alarm has been terminated. When pressed, the self-retention integrated in the drive is activated.

Title: GEZE DCU1 Manual: Automatic Door Safety & User Guide
Author: leo lu
Body HTML:
GEZE Powerdrive PL Locking Motor

2.1 For the User

Carefully read and abide by this user manual before commissioning the door, particularly when working with geze dcu1 or dcu1-nt systems. Always observe the following safety instructions:

  • Operating, maintenance and repair conditions specified by GEZE must be observed.
  • The commissioning, mandatory installation, maintenance and repair work must be performed by experts authorised by GEZE.
  • Any relevant additional country-specific and European directives must also be observed.
  • Use in dry rooms only.
  • The intervals for safety-related testing are to be complied with based on the country-specific regulations.
  • The connection to the mains voltage must be made by a professional electrician.
  • No changes may be made to the system without prior agreement from GEZE.
  • GEZE shall assume no liability for damage caused by unauthorised changes to the system.
  • The owner is responsible for safe operation of the system.
  • Have a service technician check the safe operation of the system at regular intervals.
  • Should safety devices be misaligned, thus preventing them from fulfilling their intended purpose, further operation is not permissible. The service technician must be informed without delay.
  • Make sure that the safety stickers are attached visibly to any glass leaves and are in a legible state.
  • Protect the programme switch against unauthorised access.
  • Danger of injury by sharp edges on the drive when removing the cover.
  • Danger of injury by parts hanging down.
  • This appliance can be used by children aged from 8 years and above and persons with reduced physical, sensory or mental capabilities or lack of experience and knowledge if they have been given supervision or instruction concerning use of the appliance in a safe way and understand the hazards involved.
  • Children shall not play with the appliance.
  • Cleaning and user maintenance shall not be made by children without supervision.

2.2 Intended Use

2.2.1 Automatic Door Systems

  • The sliding door system is used for the automatic opening and closing of a building passage.
  • The sliding door system may only be used in a vertical installation position and in dry rooms within the permitted application area.
  • The sliding door system is designed for pedestrian traffic in buildings.
The sliding door system is not designed for the following uses:
  • For industrial use
  • For areas of application which do not serve pedestrian traffic (such as garage doors)
  • On mobile objects such as ships

The sliding door system may only be used:

  • In the modes of operation provided for by GEZE
  • With the components approved / released by GEZE
  • With the software delivered by GEZE
  • In the installation variants / types of installation documented by GEZE
  • Within the tested/approved area of application (climate / temperature / IP rating)

Any other use is considered non-intended and will lead to the exclusion of all liability and warranty claims to GEZE.

  • The automatic sliding door system Slimdrive SL-T30 is intended for use in fire protections closer.
  • The automatic sliding door system Slimdrive SL-RD is intended for use at smoke protection doors.
  • The automatic sliding door systems Slimdrive SL RC2 and Slimdrive SC RC2 are intended for use as burglary-resistant sliding doors with Resistance class 2.
  • Only automatic FR and BO (Break-Out) sliding door systems are intended for use in escape and rescue routes.

Important information about doors in escape and rescue routes (FR drives, break-out drives)

  • Do not place objects in the passage area.
  • Existing protective door leaves/safety leaves on sliding doors must be closed again after cleaning.
  • The programme switch for changing the mode of operation on automatic door drives must be secured against activation by unauthorised persons.
  • When using a key operated programme switch, the key must be removed after changing the mode of operation.
  • The door may only be locked by authorised persons.

Description and Set-up

Drive Components

  12. Emergency control (emergency shut off switch option, emergency stop switch option)

Overview of Modes of Operation

The following modes of operation can be set on the automatic sliding doors:

  • Automatic
  • Exit only
  • Hold open
  • Night/Locked
  • Off

Settings on the Display Programme Switch (DPS)

Mode of Operation Keys / Display Explanation
Automatic aU Door opens and closes again. Inside and outside activation devices are active.
Full opening width (Indicated by LED off) Door opens the complete opening width.
Reduced opening width (Indicated by LED on) Door opens only part of the possible opening width (can be set).
Exit only (one-way operation) ls / eO / sU Internal activation device active. Outer activation device only active as long as door is not closed. Door only opens for passage from the inside to the outside.
Hold open DO / hI / op / pa Door remains open. (Not for SL RD)
Night/Locked No / NO / NI / N- Displayed until door is closed and locked (if lock is present).
(Door is closed and locked. Only “authorised” activation device is active.)
Off (service/cleaning) of Drive motor and locking are switched off. Door leaves can be moved freely by hand. Activation/safety sensors functionless.

Special Functions for FR-RWS

Mode of Operation Display Explanation
RWS N® The door is locked by the motor brake. Opening is enabled by means of the emergency stop switch.
Night/Locked No / MO / MI / N- Displayed until door is closed and locked. Opening is enabled by means of the emergency stop switch.

Settings on Keypad Programme Switch (TPS)

Mode of Operation Functionality
Automatic Door opens and closes again. Inside and outside activation devices active. Can be set to full or reduced opening width.
Exit only Internal activation device active. Outer activation device only active as long as door is not closed. Used for one-way traffic.
Hold open Door remains open. (Not for SL-RD)
Night/Locked Door is closed and locked (if lock is present). Movement detector not active. Only “authorised” activation device is active.
Off Service/maintenance position. Drive switched off. Door leaves moved freely by hand.

Operating Elements

The modes of operation can be set using the following operating elements:

  • Display programme switch DPS
  • Keypad programme switch TPS
  • Mechanical programme switch MPS with/without integrated key switch (optional)

Display Programme Switch (DPS)

Modes are set by pressing respective keys. Operation by unauthorised persons can be blocked by connection of an additional key switch or assignment of a password via usage of ST220 service menu.

Note: If a dot appears on the bottom right-hand part of the display, maintenance is due. If a dot appears on the left part, the leaf position is unknown (e.g. during teach-in).

Keypad Programme Switch (TPS)

System mode is selected and displayed on the keypad. Like the DPS, it can be secured with a key switch or password.

Mechanical Programme Switch (MPS/MPS-ST)

The mechanical switch allows mode selection via a rotary dial. The MPS is accessible to everyone, while the MPS-ST is disabled if the key is removed.

Door in Normal Operation

In normal operation (Automatic mode), the door opens and closes automatically based on sensor input.

Event / Trigger Door Reaction
Activation device triggered (push button, movement detector) Door opens and closes again.
Closing safety sensor triggered (when open) Door remains open.
Closing safety sensor triggered (when closed) Door remains closed.
Closing safety sensor triggered (while closing) Door opens again.
Opening safety sensor triggered (when closed) Door remains closed.
Opening safety sensor triggered (while opening) Door stops (or continues until reduced opening width is reached).
Obstruction contact when opening Door stops, waits, attempts to open at reduced speed three times, then closes.
Obstruction contact when closing Door reopens immediately, waits for hold-open time, then closes at reduced speed.

Special Functions

Special functions are triggered using specific switches or situations.

Switch / Function Description of Function
Authorized activation device Door opens once and closes after hold-open time. Retains set mode. If locked, it relocks in "Night/Locked".
Emergency shut-off switch Door opens once and immediately closes again.
Key switches of programme switch Locks or releases the operation of the programme switch.
Emergency stop switch Door stops and can be moved freely by hand.
Pharmacist button If equipped with toothed-belt lock, door opens a crack in "Night/Locked" mode and remains locked in this position.
Emergency lock switch Door closes and locks (if equipped with a lock).

CAUTION! Risk of injury from impact, crushing, and shearing by the door when operating the emergency lock! Ensure the switch is positioned so it can only be operated by instructed persons.

* Function only available in normal mode. If there is a fire alarm, the automatic function is deactivated and the door closes using the rubber cord (for applicable models).
